question.:question/problem:
Calculate the Cartesian equation of the circle

$$
x=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0\le \theta <2\pi .
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By squaring the $x$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {x}^{2} & ={(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By squaring the $y$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {y}^{2} & ={(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =\frac{1}{4}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{4}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(1) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the Cartesian equation is ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=\frac{1}{4}.$

By squaring the $y$-equation, we get

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}4a\cdot (b\times c) & =12 \\ 4\cdot [a\cdot (b\times c)] & =12 \\ a\cdot (b\times c) & =3.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}b\cdot (a\times c) & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $F(x,y,z)=8{z}^{2}\,i+2y\,j+k,$ what is $\text{curl}\,F?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j+R\,k$ is a vector field on ${R}^{3}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the curl of $F$ is the vector field given by

$$
curl\,F=∇\times F=\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ P & Q & R\end{vmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ 8{z}^{2} & 2y & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =[\frac{∂}{∂y}(1)-\frac{∂}{∂z}(2y)]i-[\frac{∂}{∂x}(1)-\frac{∂}{∂z}(8{z}^{2})]j+[\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y)-\frac{∂}{∂y}(8{z}^{2})]k \\  & =(0-0)i-(0-16z)j+(0-0)k \\  & =16z\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the value of ${a}_{5},$ the fifth nonzero term of the alternating series $$
\displaystyle S={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}.
$$

$$

question.:question/problem:
If the solid region $R$ is given by

$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,z)\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta .
$$

If $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z=z.
$$

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

![](images/d2/d2b3344b7b910f5685d4fd81b75a600608af6b008778ff608cb084edb5a92da9.png)

The region $R$ is one-half of a right vertical cylinder of radius $2$ whose axis passes through the point $(2,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

- bounded below by $z=0,$ and

- bounded above by $z=1.$

With that in mind, let's now write the $(x-2)^{2}+{y}^{2}=4$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-2)^{2}+{y}^{2} & =4 \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta-2)^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta)^{2} & =4 \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -4r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta+4+{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta & =4 \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )-4r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta & =0 \\ {r}^{2}-4r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta & =0 \\ r(r-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=4 \cos{\left(\theta \right)}.$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta ,z)\,:\,0\le r\le 4 \cos{\left(\theta \right)},\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{2},\,0\le z\le 1\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}x^{2} + y^{2}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}((r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta)^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta)^{2})\cdot r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta \\  & ={∭}_{Δ}{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\cdot r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}{\int }_{0}^{4 \cos{\left(\theta \right)}}{\int }_{0}^{1}r^{3}\,dz\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$
